If nothing can travel
faster than light,
could we simply cheat?
Science fiction has two
favorite shortcuts:
wormholes and warp drives.
Physicists have taken both
seriously.
And both run into
walls that may never
be broken.
First, the rule they
are trying to dodge.
Light travels at about
186,000 miles per second.
It is the universal
speed limit of cause
and effect, and nothing
with mass can ever
exceed it, or even reach it.
As an object speeds
up toward light,
every extra bit of
speed costs more energy
than the last,
and the total climbs
toward infinity.
So what about wormholes?
These Einstein-Rosen bridges
could, in theory,
connect distant regions
of spacetime, like a
tunnel through the fabric
of the universe.
But to hold a
wormhole open long enough
for anything to pass,
you would need exotic
matter with negative energy,
in amounts no one
knows how to make.
It may not exist at all.
And even then,
quantum physics may add
another hurdle.
Stephen Hawking proposed
that quantum fluctuations
could build up inside
such a tunnel and
destroy it before it
could ever be used
for time travel.
He called this the
chronology protection
conjecture.
No one knows for
sure, because we still
lack a complete theory
of quantum gravity.
Then there is the warp drive.
In 1994, physicist Miguel
Alcubierre showed
mathematically that a
spacecraft could, in theory,
travel faster than light
by contracting space in
front of it and
expanding space behind it.
Inside the warp bubble,
the ship itself is
at rest, so it
never breaks the local
speed limit.
The catch?
Early calculations said
a warp bubble would
need at least the
mass-energy of the planet
Jupiter, and it would
have to be negative energy.
Later redesigns lowered
that number, but no
one knows how to
make negative energy in
useful amounts.
Worse still, a 2012
study found that a
moving warp bubble could
sweep up particles along
the way, like a
cosmic snowplow.
When the ship stopped,
that trapped energy could
burst out ahead of
it, blasting anything
waiting at the destination.
Every escape route runs
into the same wall.
The laws of nature
are not designed for
interstellar nomads.
To see why we
are trapped inside our
cosmic neighborhood, watch
the full story on Miya's Lab.
